title: How genetic test results shape breast cancer screening and prevention
summary: A Labcorp study of nearly 4,000 women found that follow-up screening and preventive care after genetic testing varied widely depending on the gene involved.
body_markdown:
*A genetic test can reveal an inherited risk for breast cancer, but understanding what comes next is just as important.*


New Labcorp-led research, published in[JCO Precision Oncology](https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/PO-26-00373) , examined the care women received after learning they carried an inherited genetic variant linked to breast cancer risk. The study found that follow-up care varied widely depending on the gene involved, and many women did not receive screening or preventive interventions that may be recommended under clinical guidelines within the first year after testing.


## What genetic testing can reveal about breast cancer risk


While most breast cancers are not the result of inherited genetic variations, some women carry inherited **pathogenic variants** , or genetic changes, in certain genes that can increase cancer risk. The best known are ***BRCA1*** and ***BRCA2** ,* but variants in other genes may also increase the likelihood of developing breast and other cancers.


Genetic testing can identify these inherited risks, helping women and their healthcare providers make more informed decisions about screening, prevention and treatment. However, the level of risk and the recommended next steps can differ significantly depending on the gene involved.


## What happens after a genetic test identifies inherited risk?


For women with an inherited cancer risk, follow-up care may include:


- Earlier or more frequent screening, such as mammograms, breast MRI, and pancreatic screening
- Preventive options to lower breast and ovarian cancer risk, including surgery in some cases
- Genetic counseling and ongoing discussions with healthcare providers


These decisions are highly personal and often depend on factors such as age, family history, personal medical history and the specific gene involved.


##


## What the study found


Researchers analyzed data from 3,959 women who learned they carried a pathogenic variant in one of 13 genes associated primarily with breast cancer risk. Using health insurance records, they examined screening and preventive care received in the year following testing.


The findings showed that many women did not receive recommended screening or preventive care within a year of testing:


- About one-third of women received a breast MRI within a year of testing
- Fewer than 11% of eligible women underwent pancreatic cancer screening
- About one in four cancer-free women and fewer than half of women with breast cancer eligible for preventive ovarian surgery had the procedure
- Women with *BRCA1* or *BRCA2* variants were significantly more likely to undergo preventive breast surgery than those with variants in other genes. This may reflect stronger evidence and more established clinical guidelines for *BRCA1* and *BRCA2* compared with some other breast cancer susceptibility genes.


## Advancing breast cancer prevention and early detection


When breast cancer is found at an early stage, before it has spread, the five-year relative survival rate is over 99% according to the[American Cancer Society](https://www.cancer.org/content/dam/cancer-org/research/cancer-facts-and-statistics/breast-cancer-facts-and-figures/2024/breast-cancer-facts-and-figures-2024.pdf?utm_source=chatgpt.com) . That makes timely follow-up care an important next step after a genetic test result.


“A genetic test result provides important information about inherited cancer risk, but understanding how that information shapes care is just as important,” said **Emily Russell, Ph.D.,** senior manager, research studies and scientific affairs at Labcorp. “Our findings show that follow-up care can vary significantly depending on the gene involved, highlighting the need for continued research into what influences women’s care decisions after testing.”


"What this study really underscores is that a genetic test result is a starting point, not an endpoint," said **Sarah Young, M.S., CGC** , senior clinical program manager, germline oncology at Labcorp. "Knowing you carry a variant matters, but whether that knowledge translates into recommended screening or preventive care depends on many factors, and our data suggest we still have work to do to close that gap."


As genetic testing continues to expand, genetic counseling and clear, evidence-based screening recommendations can help women better understand their risk and make informed decisions about follow-up care.


**Read the study:**[Risk-Reducing Interventions in Women With Pathogenic Variants in Breast Cancer Susceptibility Genes](https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/PO-26-00373) , published in *JCO Precision Oncology*


## About the Authors


**Emily Russell, Ph.D.,** is part of Labcorp’s Genomics Sample-to-Answer Platform Center of Excellence where she leads strategic genetics research initiatives and supports a team of clinical program managers. Emily joined Invitae, now part of Labcorp, in 2021 as a Senior Data Scientist on the Medical Affairs team where her work supported evidence generation for hereditary cancer. She previously completed a postdoctoral fellowship, a Ph.D. in Human Genetics, and an MPH at the University of Pittsburgh, where her work focused on statistical genetics and the genetics of complex metabolic traits.


**Sarah Young, M.S., CGC** , is a board-certified genetic counselor with 15 years of clinical and research experience and 8 years of industry experience in oncology. Prior to joining Invitae in 2019, she was Assistant Director at the University of Chicago Center for Clinical Cancer Genetics, where her clinical and research efforts focused on rare neuroendocrine tumor syndromes, prostate cancer, and integrating genetics into routine cancer care, especially in diverse populations. At Labcorp, she leads internal and external germline oncology research efforts, with a particular interest in prostate cancer and the intersection of germline and somatic testing.


##


## Frequently Asked Questions: Inherited Breast Cancer Risk and Genetic Testing


**Q1. What are** ***BRCA1*** **and** ***BRCA2*** **genes?**
A1. *BRCA1* and *BRCA2* are the best-known genes linked to inherited breast cancer risk. Everyone has these genes, and they help repair everyday damage to the DNA inside cells. When one of them carries a pathogenic variant, the repair process may be disrupted. Over time, DNA damage can build up and increase the risk of breast, ovarian, pancreatic and other cancers.


**Q2. What is a pathogenic variant?**
A2. A pathogenic variant is a genetic change known to disrupt normal gene function. Some pathogenic variants can be inherited and increase the risk of certain cancers, including breast cancer.


**Q3. Are** ***BRCA1*** **and** ***BRCA2*** **the only genes linked to breast cancer?**
A3. No. *BRCA1* and *BRCA2* are essential markers of hereditary breast cancer risk, but they're only part of the picture. A recent study evaluated women with pathogenic variants in at least one of 13 genes linked to breast cancer risk. Each gene carries its own level of risk, and for some genes, there isn't enough research yet to guide screening and prevention.


**Q4. What is genetic testing for inherited cancer risk?**
A4. Genetic testing can detect variants in *BRCA1* , *BRCA2* , and other genes linked to cancer. Today, tests can analyze multiple genes at once, making it easier to identify inherited cancer risk. Genetic testing is often recommended for women with a personal or family history of cancer, or after a breast cancer diagnosis.


**Q5. Who should consider genetic testing for breast cancer risk?**
A5. Genetic testing is often recommended for women with a personal or family history of cancer, or after a breast cancer diagnosis. Women should talk with their healthcare provider about whether genetic testing is appropriate for their situation.


**Q6. What is the difference between screening and prevention for inherited breast cancer risk?**
A6.


- Screening aims to detect cancer earlier, often before symptoms appear. Women at higher risk may begin screening at a younger age or undergo screening more frequently. In addition to mammograms, this may include breast magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), which can detect cancers that may not be visible on a mammogram
- Prevention focuses on lowering the likelihood that cancer develops and may include preventive surgeries


**Q7. What screening options are available for women at higher risk?**
A7. Women at higher risk may begin screening at a younger age or undergo screening more frequently. Screening options include mammograms and breast MRI, which can detect cancers that may not be visible on a mammogram.


**Q8. What preventive surgeries are available for women with inherited breast cancer risk?**
A8. Preventive surgeries may include:


- Risk-reducing mastectomy: removes breast tissue to lower the risk of breast cancer
- Risk-reducing salpingo-oophorectomy: removes the ovaries and fallopian tubes to reduce the risk of ovarian cancer


**Q9. What did the Labcorp-led study find about follow-up care after genetic testing?**
A9. The study, published in[JCO Precision Oncology](https://ascopubs.org/doi/10.1200/PO-26-00373) , evaluated 3,959 women with a pathogenic variant in at least one of 13 genes linked to breast cancer risk. The group included 2,088 women without cancer and 1,871 women who had been diagnosed with breast cancer shortly before genetic testing. Key findings include:


- Only about one-third of women had a breast MRI within a year of testing
- Pancreatic cancer screening was even less common with fewer than 11% of eligible women undergoing screening
- About 1 in 4 women without cancer who met guidelines for preventive surgery had the procedure in the year after testing
- Women with *BRCA1* or *BRCA2* variants were substantially more likely to undergo preventive breast surgery than women with variants in other genes linked to breast cancer


**Q10. What factors besides genetics influenced follow-up care?**
A10. Factors beyond genetics also played a role:


- Women with a family history of cancer were more likely to have screening or surgery
- Among women without cancer, those with Medicaid were less likely than those with private insurance to have a breast MRI
- The study did not capture personal preferences or provider recommendations, both of which can shape care after testing
